hints: Focus on what the word empirical really means, the simplest whole number ratio of atoms, not the actual number of atoms.
Check each formula to see if all its subscripts can be divided by the same whole number greater than 1.
Keep the one formula that cannot be simplified any further, as that must already be in its simplest ratio form.
walkthrough:
**Recall what empirical means**

Think of empirical as simplest. It shows the lowest whole number ratio of atoms in a compound.

Rule to test:
$$\text{empirical formula = molecular formula divided to lowest ratio}$$

**Test each formula for simplification**

Look for a common divisor of all the subscripts. For $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$, all numbers divide by 2 to give $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$. For $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$, all numbers divide by 6 to give $\text{CH}_2$. For $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, both numbers divide by 2 to give $\text{HO}$.

**Spot the one that is already simplest**

For $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$, there is no whole number greater than 1 that divides 2, 4 and 1 all together. So it is already in its lowest ratio and represents an empirical formula.

options.A: Correct. In C2H4O the subscripts 2, 4 and 1 have no common divisor greater than 1, so the ratio is already in its simplest form. This is a valid empirical formula.
options.B: Incorrect. C2H4O2 can be simplified by dividing all subscripts by 2 to give CH2O. So C2H4O2 is a molecular formula, not an empirical formula.
options.C: Incorrect. C6H12 can be simplified by dividing by 6 to give CH2. Students sometimes confuse this common alkene molecular formula with an empirical formula.
options.D: Incorrect. H2O2 can be simplified by dividing by 2 to give HO. This is hydrogen peroxide, whose molecular formula is H2O2 but whose empirical formula is HO.
